schools.summary: Gill takes David's reply to Achish for the answer of a man genuinely undetermined rather than a studied evasion.
Henry sets the Philistine muster against Israel's own apostasy and reconstructs the mental reservation by which David kept himself unpromised.
Clarke and Wesley call the answer ambiguous and leave the sequel to interpret it.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch weigh the scale of the muster, the line of march, and the long consequences of David's position in Philistia.

debates.question: How should David's answer to Achish be read?

sides.position: Equivocal, with only his later conduct able to settle which way it pointed
A deliberate mental reservation, leaving the expectation standing without the promise
The reply of a man who was quite undetermined

outliers.note: Alone in reading David as undecided rather than deliberately ambiguous.

1.pericope_label: Achish said to David, Thou shalt be my bodyguard

schools.summary: Gill makes Samuel's death the hinge, explaining both the renewal of the war and the recourse to a witch.
Henry canvasses the date of the edict against the mediums and fills in what a guilty conscience supplied to Saul's fear.
Clarke notes that no accredited prophet was left to consult, and Wesley reduces the terror to a condition: closeness to God would have made the armies harmless.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch work on the terms for the two classes of practitioner and on the ground between Gilboa and Shunem.

debates.question: What lay behind Saul's terror at the Philistine army?

sides.position: The feeling that God had forsaken him, since he had beaten these enemies before
The enemy's superiority, his own army's state, and above all his state towards God
His sins set in order before his eyes, Amalekite blood spared and priestly blood spilt

outliers.note: Alone in admitting that the first term for these practitioners has never been explained with certainty.

3.pericope_label: Samuel was dead; the Philistines pitched in Shunem

schools.summary: Gill doubts the enquiry deserved the name, not being made heartily or persisted in, and notes that Saul confided only in servants he could trust.
Henry lays two charges against the errand, contempt of the God of Israel and self-contradiction after his own edict.
Clarke and Wesley gloss the woman's title bluntly, as mistress of a Pythonic spirit who converses with the devil or the dead.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott fix the term and the place, Endor surviving under its old name ten miles off past a hostile camp.

debates.question: Did Saul truly enquire of the Lord before turning elsewhere?

sides.position: Not truly or heartily, so that it was as if no enquiry had been made
He enquired and was refused, which is what drove him to the medium

outliers.note: Alone in using a modern survey of Endor and in reporting the tradition that the king's companions were Abner and Amasa.

6.pericope_label: The LORD answered him not; seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit

schools.summary: Gill explains the disguise as a common soldier's dress and marvels that a man on such an errand could swear so solemnly by the Lord.
Henry reads the disguise as degradation and finds providence in the timing, the king hearing his own edict quoted at the moment he broke it.
Clarke and Wesley add the practical fear that the woman would refuse if she knew him, and the shame of being thought guilty of the thing.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch set out what necromancy was taken to be and defend the idiom of bringing a spirit up.

sides.position: Genuine fear that the man who expelled the necromancers had sent an informer
Real danger, but also an opening to extort a larger present

outliers.note: Alone in pressing the question of what the familiar spirit was, and in noting that no other commentator here touches it.

themes: the king and his own law
8.pericope_label: Saul disguised himself and came by night; as the LORD liveth

schools.summary: Gill reports what such practitioners professed, and holds the methods withheld to check curiosity and prevent imitation.
Henry contrasts the Samuel never consulted while he lived at Ramah with the Samuel now called for, and reads the narrative's silence as deliberate.
Clarke limits the art to making a familiar personify the man named, allowing it no power over human souls at all.
Keil and Delitzsch argue from the woman's cry that she met with something essentially unlike anything her craft had produced.

debates.question: What does the woman's loud cry prove?

sides.position: That she saw an apparition she had not anticipated and could not have produced
Nothing about the apparition's nature, the narrative withholding the method on purpose

outliers.note: Alone in working out what the art could do even if founded on true principles, and in denying it any power over human souls.

11.pericope_label: Bring me up Samuel; the woman cried with a loud voice

schools.summary: Gill explains why the king may have seen nothing, the woman standing between him and the apparition.
Henry alone holds the figure to be the devil in Samuel's shape, and reads the obeisance as the stooping of a man who would not stoop to the word of God.
Clarke infers two successive apparitions and takes the plural noun for Hebrew idiom or heathen speech, and Wesley presses the dilemma that follows from denying it was Samuel.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch weigh the plural for one God-like form and ask how a spirit could be seen as an old man and clothed.

debates.question: Was the figure Samuel or a spirit personating him?

sides.position: The devil in Samuel's shape, permitted so that men who refused the truth should be deluded
Samuel himself, raised neither by the woman nor by the devil

outliers.note: The only voice here denying that Samuel appeared.

13.pericope_label: I saw gods ascending; an old man covered with a mantle

schools.summary: Gill treats the reproach as decisive against the apparition, a soul in Abraham's bosom being beyond disquieting by men or devils.
Henry finds in the complaint a man who never missed God until trouble came, and in the answer a cold comfort calculated to drive him to despair.
Clarke aims the reproach at Saul rather than the woman, and Wesley regrets only that Samuel, or rather the God of Samuel, was not called sooner.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch refuse to settle from these words what power raised the spirit, and account for the unmentioned oracle of the breastplate.

debates.question: Does the reproach settle what power raised the spirit?

sides.position: Yes: no true prophet would own such a power in magical arts
No: the words assert the disturbance and ask its reason, leaving the agent undecided

outliers.note: Alone in canvassing why the Urim goes unmentioned, preferring an answer from the Talmud to the brevity of the narrative.

15.pericope_label: Why hast thou disquieted me, to bring me up?

schools.summary: Gill takes the opening clause as spoken about David, and holds that the prediction needed no revelation.
Henry hears both charges as calculated cruelty and reckons the morrow strictly of the day then beginning.
Clarke argues the pronoun should be second person, and both he and Wesley carry a hymn stanza that hopes for more than death in the promise of company.
Ellicott divides the sentence into three judgments and reads the promise of company as a likeness of condition, not of doom.

debates.question: What does the promise that Saul would be with Samuel mean?

sides.position: No more than that he and his sons would die
A mild word of like condition in death, meant to draw him to repentance rather than crush him

outliers.note: Alone in collecting manuscript and version evidence for reading the pronoun as second person, which Ellicott calls a needless change.

17.pericope_label: The LORD hath rent the kingdom; tomorrow shalt thou be with me

schools.summary: Gill has the king fall at full length at once, as though thunderstruck.
Henry presses the fast and the conscience behind it, and judges the king terrified to despair yet never humbled.
Clarke reads the collapse as a swoon and the woman's help as common humanity, and Wesley refuses to affirm that Saul felt no contrition.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch reconstruct the posture, the night walk from Gilboa, and where the woman stood.

debates.question: Was there any contrition in Saul's collapse?

sides.position: None: terrified to despair, with no confession, sacrifice or supplication
His past sins were surely brought to mind, and no man may affirm he felt nothing

outliers.note: The only voice defending the possibility of unrecorded contrition.

20.pericope_label: Saul fell straightway all along on the earth

schools.summary: Gill states the woman's plea as an exchange of obligations and doubts the king could have eaten at all.
Henry weighs the courteous compulsion, the departure before daylight, and a hardness that never turned to repentance.
Clarke explains the speed of the cookery from the climate and closes with numbered articles holding that Samuel truly appeared.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch describe the divan, the ten miles back to Gilboa, and ascribe the woman's kindness to natural sympathy.

debates.question: Why did Saul refuse the food?

sides.position: He chose famine over the sword, dying obscurely rather than honourably
He could not eat, his stomach loathing food under grief, his appetite gone with his strength

outliers.note: Alone in denying the familiar picture of a cave, placing the scene in a house of the woman's own at Endor.

22.pericope_label: Let me set a morsel of bread before thee; they rose up and went
